q: You want a small phrase inside a paragraph to have a red background without breaking to a new line.
explain: Span is an inline element that does not force a new line layout break. Div is a block element that naturally starts on its own line.

q: Your CSS layout displays perfectly in Chrome but completely breaks in an older version of Internet Explorer.
explain: A missing doctype triggers quirks mode in older browsers, causing layout styles to render inconsistently. Adding it forces modern standards mode.

q: You add three consecutive link tags, but they all appear side-by-side instead of on new lines.
explain: Anchor tags are inline elements by default and sit next to each other. Converting them to block elements forces them to start on new lines.

q: A blind user reports that their screen reader cannot find the primary navigation area on your homepage.
explain: The semantic nav tag inherently announces its landmark role to assistive technologies. Generic tags like div provide no structural meaning to screen readers.

q: Your JavaScript click handler only works on the first button because you assigned the exact same identifier to multiple buttons.
explain: The id attribute must be completely unique within a page, causing JavaScript selectors to grab only the first match. Classes are designed for multiple items.

q: A broken image link displays a blank box on your site instead of describing what was missing.
explain: The alt attribute serves as a fallback description when an image fails to load. Title attributes only provide hover tooltips.

q: Your webpage looks incredibly tiny and zoomed out when opened on a smartphone screen.
explain: Mobile devices render desktop-sized pages and scale them down unless explicit viewport parameters are given. The viewport meta tag fixes this display behavior.

q: You want users to click a text phrase to open a contact page, but the page does not redirect.
explain: Anchor tags create clickable text hyperlinks for user navigation. Link tags specify external document relationships and belong strictly inside the head section.

q: Your bulleted list items are rendering without any indentation or bullet points on the screen.
explain: List items must be enclosed within a parent ul or ol container to format correctly. Without it, the browser fails to render standard list styling.

q: You want a link to open an external article in a completely new browser tab.
explain: The target attribute set to _blank instructs the browser to spawn a fresh window context. Rel properties handle relationship metadata instead.

q: A screen reader ignores the visual importance of text you made bold using a simple styling tag.
explain: The strong tag gives content structural semantic importance that screen readers emphasize verbally. The b tag only modifies visual weight without semantic meaning.

q: Your data table displays all cells smashed into a single line instead of separating into rows.
explain: Table data cells must be structured horizontally inside table row tags to construct vertical columns. Without row delimiters, layout alignment breaks completely.

q: Users can select multiple radio buttons simultaneously even though they should only choose one option.
explain: Radio buttons are grouped together natively by matching their name attributes. This mutual exclusion ensures only one choice remains selected at a time.

q: Your backend server receives an empty payload when a user submits a text input field.
explain: Form data keys are generated strictly from the input's name attribute during transmission. Identifying parameters like id are ignored by submission payloads.

q: Your paragraph tag automatically closes prematurely, breaking your custom layout flow in the browser DOM.
explain: Paragraph tags cannot contain block-level structures like headers or divs according to HTML specifications. Browsers automatically terminate the paragraph early when encountering them.

q: Your hidden form fields are showing up visually on the webpage layout.
explain: Setting type to hidden secures data inclusion inside forms without exposing visual input fields to layouts. CSS display properties hide elements but do not govern input behavioral frameworks.

q: The browser tab for your new web application displays the raw file path instead of a clean name.
explain: The title tag inside the head section populates the browser tab string text directly. Meta tags handle backend search descriptions or internal configs.

q: Your image breaks when moving files into a subfolder because the asset reference is hardcoded locally.
explain: Relative asset paths rely directly on the current document directory structure to resolve files. Shifting files requires modifying the folder path pointers.

q: Your background audio track refuses to play automatically when a visitor lands on the page.
explain: Modern browsers block automatic media audio playback to protect users from sudden loud noises. Adding the muted attribute bypasses this block safely.

q: Foreign accents and special characters render as broken question mark boxes across your page content.
explain: Browsers require explicit character encoding instructions to map complex symbol definitions properly. Setting UTF-8 handles international languages seamlessly.

q: A user clears an input field and completely forgets what data they were supposed to type there.
explain: Placeholder text disappears completely when typing begins, removing context for users. Semantic labels remain visible next to fields constantly.

q: Your dropdown list of countries has fifty options stacked together in one chaotic, unreadable wall of text.
explain: The optgroup tag structures long drop-down selections into labeled categories with clear visual dividers. This pattern optimizes mobile scanning significantly.

q: You want an entire product feature block to look like a card and link somewhere cleanly.
explain: HTML5 permits wrapping block-level components inside anchor tags to establish large clickable hit targets. Using click handlers relies unnecessarily on JavaScript scripts.

q: A screen reader fails to vocally emphasize a word you wrapped in an italic formatting tag.
explain: The em element marks text with relative semantic emphasis that screen readers articulate with altered tone. The i tag only stylizes visual text slants.

q: You want text layout formatting to preserve literal whitespace strings exactly as typed in your source code.
explain: Browsers collapse multiple sequential whitespaces into a single empty space by default. The pre tag instructs the parser to keep layout spacing raw.
